                    ### Question
                    A 74-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of a skin lesion on his right arm. The lesion first appeared 3 months ago and has since been slowly enlarging. Physical examination shows a 1.5-centimeter, faintly erythematous, raised lesion with irregular borders on the dorsum of the right forearm. A biopsy specimen is obtained. If present, which of the following histopathological features would be most consistent with carcinoma in situ?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Pleomorphism of cells in the stratum corneum
opb. Irreversible nuclear changes in the stratum basale
opc. Full-thickness basal to apical cell polarity
opd. Increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio in the stratum spinosum
ope. Presence of epithelial cells in the dermis

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
Carcinoma in situ is characterized by abnormal cell growth confined to the epithelium without invasion into the underlying dermis. The most relevant histopathological feature consistent with carcinoma in situ is the presence of irreversible nuclear changes in the stratum basale, indicating loss of normal differentiation. Increased nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio in the stratum spinosum can also be observed but is less specific. Pleomorphism is not specific for carcinoma in situ, and full-thickness basal to apical cell polarity suggests normal differentiation, which contradicts the diagnosis. The presence of epithelial cells in the dermis indicates invasion, which is not consistent with carcinoma in situ. Therefore, the most consistent feature with carcinoma in situ is the irreversible nuclear changes in the stratum basale.
